newsitem.title: FRANCE: Key extracts from Juppe letter to French govt.
newsitem.headline: Key extracts from Juppe letter to French govt.

text.p: Former French prime minister Alain Juppe told the new Socialist-led government when he handed over office last month that the outlook for jobs and growth was good but it needed to take tough action on public finances.

The following gives highlights of a letter from Juppe to the new government dated June 2, the day after the Socialist-led parliamentary election victory, giving key details on the outlook for growth and the state of public finances.
A copy of the letter was obtained by Reuters on Thursday.
ECONOMIC OUTLOOK

The new government would benefit from a radically different economic environment than that inherited by Juppe in 1995, due to reforms over the past two years and a recovery in the European economy, the letter said.
Public deficits were on the way down, allowing a fall in interest rates to among the lowest in the Group of Seven.
"The outlook for growth and employment are good."
Structural reforms, notably the reduction in payroll charges for the low paid, meant economic growth was producing more jobs.
"The French economy has clearly begun again to create jobs -- with a rise of 140,000 net job creations in 1997 and 250,000 next year."
The fall in inflation had led to a rise in purchasing power, supporting growth, which was expected to be 2.5 percent this year and three percent in 1998.
One question mark remained over investment, which was not taking off, though this should recover after the uncertainties surrounding the election were removed.

"Overall, everything suggests that the policies implemented as regards public finances, the fall in interest rates and the rebalancing of exchange rates have really created the conditions for a healthy and lasting recovery in activity."
1997 PUBLIC DEFICIT

"Respect for the objectives fixed for 1997 will be a significant challenge for the government...This is not definitively assured, and will require new measures, as was the case in 1996 when 25 billion francs in adjustments were made.
1997 REVENUES

"Overall the shortfall concerns revenue forecasts for a total of some 35 billion, while the spending estimates can be respected, both for the central government budget and the welfare budget, if administrators maintain their vigilance."

"The question which must be decided during the summer...is how much and by what means (savings, tapping exceptional non-fiscal revenues, questioning fiscal spending) the government will compensate for the shortfall in revenues."

Details on the revenue shortfall had not been finalised, and the total could change significantly in the months ahead depending on economic growth and employment, the letter said. The 35 billion franc shortfall was due to the following factors:
-- lower than expected revenues in 1996 had automatically reduced 1997 revenue expectations by 15 billion.
This mainly concerned a shortfall in VAT (sales tax) receipts due to the fact that economic growth had been driven by exports. Because of this, it would be a temporary phenomenon

-- the finance ministry had also commissioned an inquiry to establish whether significant VAT revenues were being lost elsewhere in the European Union due to its system of VAT collection. A report would be ready shortly
-- payroll taxes to finance welfare spending were some 10 billion francs less than expected, including a five billion franc shortfall on the main social security account
-- an agreement to redistribute most of a 12 billion franc surplus on payroll contributions to national unemployment fund UNEDIC had meant this was no longer available for the budget
1997 SPENDING
"As regards spending, additional requirements identified can be covered without major problems by lower spending on other areas," the letter said.

Finance ministry experts had estimated additional spending needs at around 23 billion francs. However some five billion francs would be saved on debt service charges if interest rates remained at their current level, while the centre-right government had also frozen 10 billion francs earlier in the year. This left only eight billion francs to be covered, on total spending of more than 1,500 billion.
ACCUMULATED WELFARE DEFICIT
This must be tackled soon to avoid reaching a limit on how much state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC) can legally advance to cover welfare system deficits.

"I must add that the question of the debt accumulated in 1996 and in the first months of 1997 must be tackled before the autumn to avoid saturation of the maximum amount available from CDC," the letter said.
1998 BUDGET
The outgoing government had planned to freeze 1998 spending at 1997 levels, in other words without a rise for inflation.

"The initial work on the budget outlook carried out by the budget ministry experts suggest a trend in public deficits to a figure above four percent of GDP, based, it is true, on particularly low forecasts for revenues," the letter said.
"This figure could be reduced to three percent after savings on budget and welfare spending, questioning some fiscal spending and tapping exceptional non-fiscal revenues," it said.
Economic growth was not having a strong enough effect on government and welfare revenues to allow the deficit to fall spontaneously.

"It is therefore certain that the credible presentation next September of a budget bill and social security bill showing a deficit of three percent will require a very strong political commitment from the whole government to limit the burden which public spending makes on our country," the letter said.
